community-s8e/u1.input:
I bring up vaccination because it's one of the values that would decide whether I could raise children in a community at all. It's not like I'm trying to design a village for everybody, but a certain amount of agreement on children's health is necessary before parents can actually trust one another.

The review from a now grown child matters more than founders usually want it to. Adults can go on forever about what they intended. The person who actually lived through the system may eventually tell a different story.
community-s8e/u1.A:
Vaccination is one of the things I would base whether I could raise kids there or not. And while I agree that the village won't be for everyone, at least for parents there needs to be some agreement on kids'health related things.

This will ultimately be reviewed by the kids, now grown. And their review will weigh more heavily, because while adults can pontificate forever, the kids might have something to say.
community-s8e/u1.B:
I specifically brought up vaccination because it is important to me, and therefore one of the values I would have to share with a community if I was going to raise my kids in that community. I'm not trying to make a community for everyone. I just think some common ground around children's health would be required if parents are going to trust each other.

Reviewer Comment: The review will come from the child(ren), who may be adults by then.

community-s8e/u2.input:
Experiments with kids sleeping and living apart from their parents need to be approached with special caution. Research on Israeli kibbutzim found that communal sleeping for children eventually came to an end, due to a combination of developmental findings, parents' preferences and social change. Kids can benefit from high-quality group care, and from having several loving adults around, but replacing a secure attachment to their parents is a different matter.

Tamera's Children's Place deserves to be studied directly, not caricatured. Personally, I'm still biased toward systems that open up a kid's circle without making the bond between parent and child ideologically inconvenient.
community-s8e/u2.A:
I do think that one has to be really careful about doing experiments that could hinder that, like the ones that some people want to do in regards to kids sleeping and living separate from parents. The experiments done on the Israeli Kibbutzim ended up not working out and they ended the practice of kids sleeping communally for a variety of reasons - developmental, parental and social. I do think kids can benefit from high quality communal care and many loving adults in their lives but that shouldn't be a substitute for kids having a secure attachment to their parents.

People would have to look at what is going on at the Children's Place at Tamera to get an idea about how it works but my biased opinion is that I prefer a system where kids are exposed to more people but where their relationship with their parents is not ideologically antithetical.
community-s8e/u2.B:
In general I'd say this kind of experiments, where kids don't sleep and live with their parents, need a lot of caution. For instance the practice of kids sleeping together in the Israeli kibbutzim had its end, due to the combined effects of new findings in developmental psychology, the wishes of the kids' parents and other social changes. Kids profit from high quality group care and a variety of loving adults in their life, but this should not hinder them from creating a secure attachment to their parents.

Still, I'm very interested to see what the Children's Place in Tamera is about and (being the biased person I am) hope that it is a system, that allows for an expanded circle for kids, without being ideologically inconvenient for the kids and their parents : )

community-s8e/u3.input:
Kids also need their own territory, a space to create their own society in, invent games and work out ordinary disputes, without always being under the management of adults.

I got a taste of that at a Unitarian youth camp, and it's still one of the freest memories I have. ZEGG's Kinderhaus works from a similar idea. The adults take care of safety on the outside, but the kids still get a world of their own.
community-s8e/u3.A:
Kids need their own territory where they can create their own society, make up their own games, fight each other, etc.

One of my freest memories is from a unitarian youth camp, so I know what it's like. (In ZEGG's Kinderhaus the kids also have their own world as long as they are safe from the outside world.)
community-s8e/u3.B:
Kids need territory, where they can build their own little society and invent their own games and deal with their problems amongst themselves, without being constantly managed by adults.

My most free memory is from a Unitarian youth camp. And that is how the kids house at ZEGG is as well – the adults make sure that it is safe outside, but inside the kids have a world of their own.

community-s8e/u4.input:
Because this can be badly misunderstood, the safeguards have to be spelled out. A children's territory can't become a place where adults stop paying attention. It can't be a place where older kids quietly dominate younger ones, or where secrecy gets treated as a sign of independence.

I also don't buy the suburban paranoia that treats any warm relationship between a kid and a grownup who isn't related to them as suspect. It's good for a child to know and be known by lots of grownups who enjoy them, who would notice when something changes, and who would act when something's wrong. That kind of fear can destroy the gift without actually preventing abuse.
community-s8e/u4.A:
There are a few caveats here that could be twisted into something sinister if I don't lay them out. First of all, I'm not talking about creating territory for children where adults can't go, or allowing older children to control the territory of younger ones, and I'm not talking about secretiveness.

Second, I don't think it's helpful for adults, living in their secure suburban enclaves, to be so afraid of child molestation that they inhibit affectionate relationships between children and non-related adults. It's good for children to have lots of adults who love them in their lives, and who would spring into action if the need arose.
community-s8e/u4.B:
Mind, I imagine that might come out wrong, so I’d put a lot of safeguards on what I mean by a place for children – it can’t be unmonitored by adults, or a place where older children can lord it over younger ones, or secretive.

And I think it’s a real problem that so many suburban folks are afraid to let their children be close to anyone who isn’t related to them. It is a GOOD thing for kids to have a whole bunch of people who know them and like them and would notice if something bad were happening to them, and act.

community-s8e/u5.input:
The protection has several parts:

Give children real agency. Their "no" matters. No grown-up has a right to a child's affection, physical contact, obedience beyond what legitimate safety requires, or private access to them.

Have a no-secrets rule. No grown-up may ever ask a child to keep a gift, a game, a touch, a conversation, or a relationship secret from the child's mother or another trusted adult. A surprise needs an end date. Secrets meant to isolate the child aren't allowed.
community-s8e/u5.A:
There are a few parts to it:

- Children are the masters of their own bodies, their "no" is valid and a grownup can never ever demand, expect or believe they have a right to their love, physical contact, unconditional compliance (outside of legitimate safety concerns) or access.

- No grownup can ever tell a child they need to keep a secret from their mother or other grownups that the child trusts. This includes keeping secret any gift or present, playing a certain game, being touched, spending time together, or anything else. While surprises need an eventual end date, no grownup can ever ask a child to keep a secret in order to separate the child from the support of those who are there for the child.
community-s8e/u5.B:
Here are a few of those parts:

Children have the right to say "No." No grownup has a right to a child's love, a child's body, a child's obeying, or access to a child. (Of course, there are needs to obey for legitimate safety needs.)

No grownup may ever make a child keep a secret from his mom or from anyone else the child trusts. No grownup may ever give a child a gift, play a game, touch a child, talk to a child, or be with a child and say, "Don't tell anyone about this." Even surprises have to have an ending date when they are told. No grownup may ever want to keep a child a secret from anyone.

community-s8e/u6.input:
Teach kids to be truthful before there's a crisis. They should know that what they say is powerful, and that adults will listen seriously. That teaching must never turn into an interrogation, punishment for not being sure, or a reason to dismiss what a child reports. A scared or confused child may not tell the story perfectly, and still need protecting.

Hear the child even when the person accused is someone people love. That's where communities fail, because the adult may be charismatic, useful, rich, spiritually important, or just everybody's friend. Decide on the process for responding ahead of time, before anyone's face is attached to it. First, make sure everyone is safe right away. Then see that a competent and fair investigation is done, and that nothing gets hushed up because of anybody's status.
community-s8e/u6.A:
Do a great job with the kids. Teach them that telling the truth is important, that their words have power, and that people will take what they say seriously and respond appropriately. Don't interrogate them or punish them if they aren't sure of everything or tell the story "wrong." Just help them to be truth tellers. And be ready to act in their protection.

Do a great job listening to the kids even when they point an finger at someone that the community loves. The community often fails in this area because the accused is charismatic, brings in a lot of money, is a great spiritual leader, is everyone's best friend, etc. Be clear about the process ahead of time. Do whatever is necessary immediately to keep everyone safe and then be sure that the situation is investigated competently and fairly. Don't cover it up.
community-s8e/u6.B:
First, as a parent, teach all of the kids that being truthful is super-important and powerful. Be careful not to interrogate or punish them if they don't get it 100% right the first time, or if they don't describe the story just the way a pro would. They need to know that whatever they say will be taken seriously and that they will be protected no matter what.

Second, when a child tells a story, listen to them, even when the person they are accusing is someone loved by the community. This is the place where most communities fail, because the person is charismatic, doing good work, rich, important, a friend, etc. Have a process in place before the situation arises to make sure that, first, all are protected, and second, that a competent and fair investigation takes place and isn't hushed up.

community-s8e/u7.input: Make sure kids have relationships and a reporting route outside the community. Grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers and other trusted adults give them perspective on their life, and someone to talk to. Make sure there's at least one trusted adult, advocate or reporting route they can reach without going through the community's leadership. In 1984, Vermont authorities seized 112 children in the Island Pond raid, and a court returned them after rejecting the state's blanket request. State intervention can fail spectacularly. A community that closes itself off completely can also fail. Children need more than one world.
community-s8e/u7.A: It is critical that children raised in a community keep ties to the outside world. A close relationship with grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers, or other community members is very important for perspective. The existence of at least one trusted adult, advocate, or reporting avenue to people outside of the leadership of the community is important. A total reliance on the state to protect children is not warranted, as the failed 1984 raid on the Island Pond, Vermont community where authorities took 112 children and were forced by a court to return them demonstrates. But a total closing off to the outside world is probably not desirable either.
community-s8e/u7.B: Whatever else, ensure that the kids are maintaining relationships outside the community. Whether that means grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers or other trusted adults, kids need to have some perspective on their life, some context, and some way of reporting problems to someone. As long as there is at least one adult the kids can trust, advocate for them or to whom they can report what is going on. Sure, the state is supposed to be such an entity, but as the Island Pond raid demonstrated, they can fail. In that raid in Vermont in 1984, state authorities seized 112 children but a court sent them back after rejecting a blanket request by the state, so it's not a complete solution. Total closure doesn't work either. Kids need multiple worlds.

community-s8e/u8.input: I also searched the research corpus for a well-documented case of a child in an intentional community who remained seriously dangerous to other people, where the record follows the whole sequence of events: the conduct, the assessment, the intervention, the review, and what happened later. I didn't find one. That may be because records are private, or because cases were sent elsewhere, but it means I can't claim that communities already know how to handle the hardest version on their own. The child, the family, and the people at risk all need access to competent help and review that the home community doesn't control.
community-s8e/u8.A: Further, I don't think that there is an example in this corpus of research of an actual case of a child in an intentional community who was seriously dangerous to people, and for whom there is a good record of all the steps taken to deal with the situation. It may be that the issue has come up, but was either handled in private or by removing the case to a different community. In any case, it seems to me that the child, the family, and the potential targets of dangerous behavior all deserve access to competent help and review, outside the control of the home community.
community-s8e/u8.B: I have recently searched the corpus of research for a single well-documented case involving a child raised in an intentional community who was seriously dangerous to other human beings, where the entire sequence of events was well documented. I failed to find such a case. This is why I argue that even if one lived in such a community, one should make sure that the child and the family (and, indeed, any other potential objects of the child's dangerous behavior) have access to competent assistance and review which is not under the control of one's home community.

community-s8e/u9.input:
Amish young people decide for themselves, as adults, whether or not to join the church, and roughly 85 percent or more eventually do. Popular culture has blown Rumspringa out of proportion, as if every teenager went wild, but adult baptism still matters, because it makes belonging a commitment instead of a fact imposed at birth.

If a community's children never leave, how can it know whether they'd freely come back? Let them study, travel, make friends, run into other ways of life, and disagree with the founders without being treated as traitors.
community-s8e/u9.A:
Yes, the Amish do allow their youth to decide whether or not to join the church on their own. 85% or more do, but popular culture has a tendency to blow the Rumspringa out of proportion. The reason they wait until adulthood to be baptised is because it means more when it isn't forced on them.

If the children never leave how will they ever come back? Allow them to study, travel, befriend and counter-act the ideologies of the founder, and they wont feel like traitors for it.
community-s8e/u9.B:
The interesting thing is, they are allowed to do whatever they want until they are old enough to make the decision themselves, and 85% (or is it more? hmm...) of them DO choose to become part of the church. It's only in pop culture that the "Rumspringa" period has been blown out of proportion. And there's a lot to be said for being an adult when being baptized.

If all of the children of a community join it, then how can they be certain that they are joining of their own free will? Allow them to experience other things, to learn, to travel, to befriend people, to disagree with the teachings of the founder.

community-s8e/u10.input: Every childhood narrows the future. Most ordinary parents aren't going to give their kid a bunch of money at 18 and say, "Go see the world." They'll try to get them ready for some next step that can actually work. A poor or money-free community may have even less cash to offer, and food, medical care and basic survival may rightly come first.
community-s8e/u10.A: It also depends on how they were raised, their family and what their community is like. Most normal people aren't going to give their kid a bunch of money when they turn 18 and tell them to go travel the world and see everything. Most people try to help their kid prepare for the next step that they know will work. If they are from a poor community, or a community with no money, food, medical care and overall survival might be more important.
community-s8e/u10.B: It is the nature of things that childhood narrows down the possible futures for a human being. Unless the kid is wealthy, it's very unlikely that the parents are going to give the kid a bag full of money when they turn 18, and say "Go out there and see the world, son!". If the parents are of common or even poor background, it's more likely that they will want the kid to work towards the next logical step in their life. If the kid comes from a community with little to no money, it's possible that getting food and medical care might be the main concern.

community-s8e/u11.input: The realistic standard isn't unlimited freedom. It's that leaving shouldn't be made artificially impossible. Kids who grow up without using money especially need to know enough about how the money world works that they aren't helpless in it: jobs, rent, contracts, banking, scams, ID, getting around, and how to ask for help. They need skills and an education they can take with them, relationships outside the community, access to their records and documents, and at least one plausible next step, whether that's school, an apprenticeship, work, family or another community. If the community can help out with temporary housing, travel, tools, or a small reserve for the transition, great. But even if it can't, it can at least avoid punishing people for leaving, or withholding the knowledge and records a young adult needs to function somewhere else. No upbringing gives perfect freedom. The point isn't to erase path dependence. It's to not turn belonging into a trap.
community-s8e/u11.A: The important thing isn’t total, complete freedom, but rather getting to the somewhat more realistic standard of not making it impossible . For kids that never lived in the money world, this means teaching them about the money world, teaching them how to navigate it, giving them as much education and skill as possible, giving them some way out – a place to go, whether it be a school, or apprenticeship, or job, or family, or other community, and giving them some flexibility – maybe in the form of temporary housing, or travel, or some tools, or a bit of money, or whatever. If the community can’t give them any flexibility, that’s unfortunate, but at least the community shouldn’t punish them for leaving, and should give them all their records and whatnot. Total freedom is not possible due to path dependancy, but it’s possible to not be a prison.
community-s8e/u11.B: And the realistic standard for this is not that insane one that some are implying here. The realistic standard is just that it is not artificially impossible to leave. And that’s harder than it sounds if people grew up with no exposure to how the money world works. They need to be taught about that world and made aware of it. They need to be given relevant skills and education that are applicable in the outside world. They need to be allowed to form social connections with people outside the community. They need to be given access to their records and documents. They need to be given some path out in the first place, like to school, or to an apprenticeship, or to a job, or to family, or to another community. They can even be given material help to smooth the transition. But even if they’re not, there are a lot of things that a community can do to help people leave, or at the very least not make it artificially harder for them to leave. No upbringing gives someone complete freedom, but at least the path dependence can be minimized.

community-s8e/u12.input:
Some may leave for good, and others may start their own communities with different values instead of waiting decades to inherit the original one. Parents may feel that as a loss, even when it's the movement evolving.

Couples who share a home, a culture and a bed still split over screens, vaccines, schooling, religion, food, discipline and medical care. Now multiply that by twenty adults with twenty different childhoods.

Goodwill doesn't answer those questions once there are children in the middle of the disagreement. Communities need enough shared principles about raising children to offer coherence, and enough room for parents to still be parents.
community-s8e/u12.A:
It’s quite possible some of them will leave. It’s quite possible some of them will start their own communities and be done with waiting for decades to inherit this one, because the values are different enough that the kids don’t want to inherit this community when it comes time. And that will feel like loss to some of the parents, too.

People who live together, come from the same culture, sleep in the same bed, form a family together can split apart over “screen time” and vaccines and schooling and religion and what to feed the kids and how to discipline them and what kinds of medical care they should or should not get. It’s even more possible with twenty adults who all have different childhoods.

Goodwill isn’t enough once kids are involved. There needs to be enough shared principles about kids to give the community some coherence, but enough space for parents to be parents.
community-s8e/u12.B:
What's to stop them leaving altogether, or setting up their own communities elsewhere with different values, instead of sticking around to inherit the original community in due course ? Won't that be felt by their parents to be a loss ?

People who live together in the same house, from the same culture, sharing a bed, can't agree on screens, vaccines, schooling, religion, food, discipline, medical, etc etc - just think what happens when 20 adults, all with different childhood experiences, want to agree on these issues for their children.

It won't be enough for everyone to just want the best for each others' children, or to 'approach things in good faith', etc. There needs to be some common ground - not so much that it prevents the parents from being able to parent, but enough that there is some coherence to the community.
